title: Tolan v. Cotton (2014)
summary: The lower court had to assess the officer’s motion using reasonable inferences favorable to the injured plaintiff.
notes:
This is a short assigned note. It supplies a useful limit on overly broad readings of Scott: a judge may not treat ordinary disagreement in testimony as an absence of a genuine dispute.

The Supreme Court's decision was per curiam. Robert Tolan, unarmed, was shot on his parents' front porch by Sergeant Jeffrey Cotton on New Year's Eve 2008; the suit was under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for excessive force, and the summary-judgment ruling arose on the officer's qualified-immunity defense.

The Court faulted the Fifth Circuit for failing to adhere to the axiom that on summary judgment "[t]he evidence of the nonmovant is to be believed, and all justifiable inferences are to be drawn in his favor."

sections.Parties: Tolan brought an excessive-force claim against officer Cotton after a shooting.
sections.Material Facts: The record contained disputes about lighting, Tolan’s mother’s demeanor, whether Tolan’s words were threatening, and his position when shot. The lower court credited accounts supporting the officer while failing to acknowledge significant contrary evidence from Tolan’s side.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment and the Fifth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court vacated and remanded.
sections.Issue: Did the lower court evaluate the disputed evidence consistently with the summary-judgment standard?
sections.Holding: No. It had to credit the nonmovant’s competent evidence and draw reasonable inferences in his favor.
sections.Reasoning: Different witnesses bring perceptions and possible biases, and genuine disputes among their accounts generally belong to the factfinder. The Court identified specific instances in which the lower court resolved those disputes for the movant. Correcting that error required reconsideration of qualified immunity on the appropriate view of the evidence. The Supreme Court did not itself decide that the officer violated clearly established law.

learning.why: The lower court had to assess the officer’s motion using reasonable inferences favorable to the injured plaintiff.

topics.cp-inferences: The lower court failed to credit the nonmovant’s evidence about disputed circumstances of the shooting.
topics.cp-judge-jury: Weighing witness accounts against the nonmovant exceeded the summary-judgment role.
topics.cp-summary-judgment: The case is a direct application of the Rule 56 standard and is taught as the Court's reminder that courts may not weigh evidence at summary judgment.
topics.cp-frcp-56: The decision turns on the Rule 56 genuine-dispute standard applied to the officer's motion.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Alito, joined by Justice Scalia, agreed that genuine factual disputes existed but questioned using Supreme Court review to correct this ordinary application of a settled standard.
